_meta.notes: Scores: capacity, output, solar and portability are formula-based (see /how-we-rate/); charging, longevity and value are editorial. Null = not published/verified.

products.name: BLUETTI Elite 10 Mini

specs_extra.Air travel: 128 Wh — under the 160 Wh limit most airlines allow in carry-on (with airline approval above 100 Wh)
specs_extra.Light: Built-in LED with warm, cool and SOS modes

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (128 Wh, 200 W AC, 100 W USB-C, 150 W AC charge in 70 min, 100 W solar, 3.97 lb). Cycle rating and warranty aren't on the listing.

editorial.tagline: A 4 lb power bank with a real AC outlet and a 10 ms UPS.
editorial.summary: 128 Wh in a 4 lb box: one 200 W AC outlet, 100 W USB-C, a 10 ms UPS for a router or laptop, and a 70-minute recharge. It's a big power bank, not a backup for appliances.
body: The Elite 10 Mini sits between a power bank and a power station. At 128 Wh it holds about four large power banks' worth of energy, and the single 200 W AC outlet runs a laptop, a camera charger or a small fan.

It's small enough for a backpack and under the 160 Wh carry-on limit, and the 10 ms UPS makes it a tidy backup for a Wi-Fi router or a desk setup. It refills in 70 minutes from the wall or from a 100 W panel.

Owners like it for kids' tablets, travel and overnight desk fans. One long-term owner hit a battery fault after charging it from a car inverter, and many reviews on the listing are for BLUETTI's older AC2A.
pros: 10 ms UPS for router or laptop
cons: Warranty and cycle rating not listed
editorial.ideal_for: Travel, remote work from a café or car, and keeping a router alive through short outages.
editorial.not_for: Fridges, CPAP with a heated humidifier or anything that draws more than 200 W.
editorial.verdict: The best 'big power bank' here — just don't expect it to back up your home.
editorial.review_summary: 4.3★ from 1,263 ratings (84% 4–5 stars). Owners use it for tablets, laptops, headsets and desk fans overnight. One 4-star owner reports a battery-management fault after charging from a car inverter. Some reviews on the listing are for the older BLUETTI AC2A.

reviews.excerpt: Small and powerful; the kids fight over it for tablets and headsets.

reviews.author: Bryan

reviews.author: W. Costley

products.name: ALLWEI 300W Portable Power Station

specs_extra.Outputs: 1 AC (pure sine), 2 DC5521, car socket, USB-A 18 W, USB-C 60 W
specs_extra.Solar: 4–5 h with a 100 W panel (max input not listed)

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (256 Wh LiFePO4, 3,000 cycles, 300 W / 600 W surge, 6.4 lb, 2-year warranty).

editorial.tagline: The cheapest LiFePO4 power station worth buying.
editorial.summary: 256 Wh of long-life LiFePO4 and a 300 W pure-sine outlet for about $130 — enough for a CPAP without heat for two to three nights, a router through an outage or phones and lights on a camping trip.
body: ALLWEI's 300 W unit is as simple as power stations get: one AC outlet, a 60 W USB-C port, DC barrel jacks and a car socket, wrapped around a 256 Wh LiFePO4 battery rated for 3,000 cycles.
The trade-off for the price is charging speed: 3.5 to 4 hours from the wall and 4 to 5 hours from a 100 W panel. There's no app and no UPS mode.

Owners report running a CPAP without heat for about 20 hours over three nights, and one mountain owner bought three to ride out wind-related shutoffs. A few note the battery gauge can drop suddenly near empty.
editorial.ideal_for: A first backup for a router, CPAP (no heat) or phones, on a tight budget.
editorial.not_for: Anyone who needs to recharge quickly or run more than 300 W.
editorial.verdict: The best cheap power station: slow to charge, but long-lived and honest.
editorial.review_summary: 4.4★ from 2,450 ratings (85% 4–5 stars). Owners praise build quality, quiet operation and real-world CPAP runtime. One 4-star owner saw the battery gauge fall from 99% to low suddenly.

products.name: GRECELL EB500 Portable Power Station

specs.charge_note: 6–9 h with a 100 W panel; owners report a ~105 W limit on solar/DC input

specs_extra.Outputs: 2 AC (pure sine), USB-C 60 W, 3 USB-A QC 18 W, DC ports — 10 devices at once
specs_extra.Listing name: Sold as 'Portable Power Station 500W 519.48Wh'; brand GRECELL, model EB500

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (519 Wh, 500 W / 1,000 W surge, 2 AC, 2-year warranty; 18 lb as listed). Cell chemistry and cycle rating are not stated; solar limit from owner reviews.

editorial.tagline: 519 Wh for $180 — the most capacity per dollar under $200.
editorial.summary: Twice the capacity of the 300 Wh units for about the same money, with two 500 W pure-sine outlets. The catch: slow charging, an unstated battery chemistry and a third-party seller.
body: GRECELL's EB500 is sold on Amazon under a generic title, but it's a straightforward 519 Wh box with two pure-sine AC outlets (500 W, 1,000 W surge), 60 W USB-C and three quick-charge USB-A ports.

At $180 that's about $0.35 per Wh, cheaper than anything else under $500. The listing doesn't say whether the cells are LiFePO4, and owners report that solar and car charging top out around 105 W, so a full recharge takes most of a day.
Recent buyers like the price and the carry handle; a craft-show vendor ran two lamps for nine hours with 40% left. Some reviews on the listing are for older GRECELL models.
cons: Heavier than LiFePO4 rivals of this size
editorial.ideal_for: Occasional use — craft fairs, camping lights, a router during short outages — on a strict budget.
editorial.not_for: Daily cycling, fast turnarounds or anyone who wants a long-life LiFePO4 battery.
editorial.verdict: The most capacity for the money under $200, if you can live with slow charging.
editorial.review_summary: 4.5★ from 246 ratings (86% 4–5 stars). Buyers praise the price, light and simplicity. Complaints: long charging time and a ~105 W limit on solar/DC input. Some reviews cover older GRECELL models.

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (292 Wh LiFePO4, 300 W / 600 W surge, 100 W USB-C, 7.5 lb, 4,000 cycles to 70%, 2-year warranty on the listing).

editorial.tagline: Amazon's best-selling power station, now with LiFePO4.
editorial.summary: 292 Wh, two AC outlets, 100 W USB-C and a 4,000-cycle LiFePO4 battery in a 7.5 lb box. Slow to recharge from the wall, but proven by more than 11,000 ratings.
body: The Explorer 300 is the most-bought power station on Amazon. The current version uses LiFePO4 cells rated for 4,000 cycles to 70%, and weighs 7.5 lb with a built-in handle.

It runs laptops, cameras, drones, lights and a CPAP without heat; 300 W isn't enough for a clothes steamer or a kettle. Wall charging takes about four hours, which is slow next to newer rivals that refill in an hour.
Owners use it for camping, market stalls and events several times a week, and the review history goes back years. If you don't need fast charging, it's a safe, simple pick.
cons: About 4 h to recharge from the wall
editorial.ideal_for: Camping, vendors and a CPAP (no heat) for one or two nights.
editorial.not_for: Anyone who needs a fast recharge or runs anything above 300 W.
editorial.verdict: The safe, proven small pick — pay a little more for faster charging elsewhere.
editorial.review_summary: 4.6★ from 11,269 ratings (90% 4–5 stars). Owners praise portability, reliability and how many devices it keeps charged. A 4-star owner notes it wouldn't run a clothes steamer, which exceeds 300 W.

products.name: BLUETTI Elite 30 V2

specs_extra.Power Lifting: Runs resistive loads up to 1,500 W at reduced power

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (288 Wh, 600 W, 1,500 W lifting, 10 ms UPS, 380 W AC charge, 5-year warranty) + Solar Waypoint (200 W solar, 3,000 cycles).

editorial.tagline: Twice the output of other 300 Wh units, plus a real UPS.
editorial.summary: 600 W from a 288 Wh LiFePO4 battery, a 10 ms UPS, 140 W USB-C and a 70-minute recharge, backed by a 5-year warranty — for under $300.
body: Most power stations this size stop at 300 W. The Elite 30 V2 delivers 600 W continuous, so it can run a small blender or a heated CPAP humidifier, and Power Lifting keeps some higher-wattage resistive loads going at reduced power.
It charges to 80% in 45 minutes and full in 70 from the wall, and its 10 ms UPS switch makes it a good compact backup for a router, a home server or a CPAP.
Owners use it at card shows, off-grid cabins and on camping trips. At 9.5 lb it's a little heavier than the Jackery 300, and solar input tops out at 200 W.
editorial.ideal_for: A small UPS for a router, server or CPAP, and fast-turnaround camping.
editorial.not_for: Long outages — you'll need 1 kWh or more for a fridge.
editorial.verdict: The best power station under $300: fast, powerful for its size and a real UPS.
editorial.review_summary: 4.5★ from 1,182 ratings (86% 4–5 stars). Owners use it as a home-server UPS, for vendor displays and on camping trips, and praise the charging speed. A few say it's heavier than they expected.

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (286 Wh, 600 W / 1,200 W X-Boost, 3 AC, <10 ms UPS, 1 h AC charge, 220 W solar, expandable to 858 Wh, 7.7 lb, 5-year warranty).

editorial.tagline: A 7.7 lb UPS that grows to 858 Wh.
editorial.summary: 286 Wh with three AC outlets, a 10 ms UPS with PC shutdown support, a one-hour recharge and an add-on battery option that nearly triples capacity.
body: The RIVER 3 Plus is EcoFlow's small all-rounder: 600 W from three AC outlets, 100 W USB-C, a car socket and a 30 dB fan. It refills in an hour from the wall or 1.5 hours on 220 W of solar.

Its standout is expansion: clip on an EB300 or EB600 battery and capacity grows to 858 Wh, enough for a 12 V cooler over a festival weekend. The UPS switches in under 10 ms and includes a USB cable so a PC or NAS can shut down cleanly.
Owners have replaced traditional UPS boxes with it and run 12 V coolers overnight. With 368 ratings it has a shorter track record than the Jackery 300, and it's sold directly by EcoFlow.
pros: 10 ms UPS with PC shutdown cable
editorial.ideal_for: Desk and network UPS duty, and campers who may want more capacity later.
editorial.not_for: Anyone who needs to run appliances above 600 W.
editorial.verdict: The best small UPS here, with room to grow.
editorial.review_summary: 4.4★ from 368 ratings (84% 4–5 stars). Owners use it as a server UPS and to run 12 V coolers overnight, and like the fast charging. Several note you must size it correctly for your loads.

specs_extra.USB-C: Two 140 W two-way USB-C (can also charge the station), plus a 15 W USB-C

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (288 Wh, 300 W / 600 W surge, 2×140 W USB-C, 80% in 50 min, 25 dB, 5-year warranty) + Solar Waypoint (100 W solar, 330 W AC input, 10 ms UPS).

editorial.tagline: A quiet power station built around two 140 W USB-C ports.
editorial.summary: 288 Wh, three AC outlets and two 140 W two-way USB-C ports in a tall, compact 9 lb body. It's whisper-quiet at 25 dB and backed by a 5-year warranty, but costs more than rivals with twice the output.
body: The C300 is built for laptops and gadgets: two 140 W USB-C ports (PD 3.1) can fast-charge big laptops or recharge the station itself, and three AC outlets share 300 W.
It reaches 80% in 50 minutes from the wall and doubles as a 10 ms UPS. Fan noise is rated at 25 dB, among the quietest here, which matters for a bedside CPAP.
Owners call it neat and well built, and several use it as a desk UPS. At $330 it's pricier than the Elite 30 V2, which has twice the AC output.
editorial.ideal_for: Laptop-heavy travel, a quiet bedside CPAP (no heat) and desk UPS duty.
editorial.not_for: Anything that draws more than 300 W.
editorial.verdict: The best USB-C hub here — but the Elite 30 V2 is better value for AC loads.
editorial.review_summary: 4.6★ from 1,913 ratings (91% 4–5 stars). Owners praise the build quality, compact size and three standard AC outlets, and several use it as a UPS. One notes it's great 'unless you need serious consistent power'.

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W / 2,700 W, 1,440 W AC charge, 500 W solar, 5-year warranty, 37.4 lb) + Solar Waypoint (20 ms UPS, 3,000 cycles).

editorial.tagline: 1,152 Wh for $449 — the cheapest real 1 kWh station here.
editorial.summary: More capacity than the $499 1 kWh rivals for less money: 1,800 W output, a one-hour recharge, 500 W solar input and a 5-year warranty, sold by Amazon. It's heavier than the newer models.
body: The AC180 is a slightly older design, which is why it costs less: 1,152 Wh of LiFePO4 and 1,800 W from four AC outlets, with Power Lifting to 2,700 W for heaters and kettles.
It charges at up to 1,440 W from the wall (80% in 45 minutes) and accepts 500 W of solar. The UPS switch is 20 ms, fine for routers and most PCs but slower than the 10 ms units.

At 37.4 lb it's 12 lb heavier than the Elite 100 V2 or Anker C1000 Gen 2. Owners run car fridges for five-day camping trips and use it for work-from-home backup; one points out the inverter itself draws about 15 W.
pros: Full recharge in about an hour
editorial.ideal_for: Home backup for a fridge, router and lights, and car camping with a 12 V fridge.
editorial.not_for: Anyone who carries it often.
editorial.verdict: The best value per watt-hour among the 1 kWh stations — if you don't mind the weight.
editorial.review_summary: 4.6★ from 2,620 ratings (90% 4–5 stars). Owners call it easy to use and reliable for camping, RVs and outages. One owner notes the ~15 W inverter draw reduces runtime on light loads; another was disappointed by the wireless charging pad.

editorial.tagline: The best-selling 1 kWh station: light, simple and proven.
editorial.summary: 1,070 Wh and 1,500 W in a 23.8 lb box that charges in an hour, with thousands of owner reviews behind it. It has fewer outlets and less solar input than the newest rivals.
body: Jackery's 1000 v2 is the 1 kWh model most people buy. It's light for its class at 23.8 lb and runs a fridge, a CPAP with humidifier, a coffee maker or small power tools on 1,500 W (3,000 W surge).
Charging takes 1.7 hours by default, or one hour in the app's emergency mode; a quiet 30 dB overnight mode is also available. Solar input tops out at 400 W, and it has three AC outlets.
Owners use it for CPAP backup, keeping a boat's shore power going at anchor and art-festival booths, and the rating is among the highest here at 4.7 from 3,600+ reviews.
editorial.ideal_for: CPAP backup, weekend camping and first-time buyers who want a proven brand.
editorial.not_for: Solar-heavy setups or anyone who needs more than 1,500 W.
editorial.verdict: The safest 1 kWh pick — the Anker C1000 Gen 2 does more for the same price.
editorial.review_summary: 4.7★ from 3,621 ratings (93% 4–5 stars). Owners use it for CPAP machines, outages, boats and events, and praise the light weight and easy app. Several compare it closely with EcoFlow's Delta series.

editorial.tagline: EcoFlow's DELTA 3 without expansion, for $100 less.
editorial.summary: 1,024 Wh, 1,800 W (3,600 W surge), a 10 ms UPS, 500 W solar and a 45-minute charge to 80% — the core DELTA 3 experience at $499, minus the extra-battery port.
body: The DELTA 3 Classic keeps what most people use: 1,800 W from four AC outlets, X-Boost for resistive loads up to 2,600 W, a 10 ms UPS for PCs and medical devices and fast X-Stream charging (80% in 45 minutes).
What you give up versus the $599 DELTA 3 is expansion — it can't take extra batteries — and a few outputs. Solar input is the same 500 W.
Owners power van-life setups, wedding photo booths and printers, and home outages; the only frequent complaint is the 26.7 lb weight. Its 90% five-star share is the highest in our catalog.
cons: Heavier than Anker and BLUETTI rivals
Cycle rating not stated on the listing

editorial.not_for: Anyone who may want to add capacity later.
editorial.verdict: Our favorite all-rounder at $499 — as long as you don't need to expand it.

editorial.tagline: 1 kWh with 1,000 W of solar input — double its rivals.
editorial.summary: A compact 25 lb 1 kWh station with 1,800 W output, a 10 ms UPS, a 30 dB silent mode and 1,000 W of solar input, which refills it in about an hour and a half of good sun.
body: The Elite 100 V2 matches the Jackery and EcoFlow 1 kWh models on capacity and output (1,800 W, 3,600 W surge), but accepts up to 1,000 W of solar — twice the DELTA 3 Classic and 2.5 times the Jackery.
It's also the most compact of the group at 17 liters and 25 lb, charges to 80% in about 45 minutes, runs at 30 dB in silent mode and switches to battery in 10 ms.
Owners use it for camping, off-grid trips and as a 'bridge' before starting a gas generator. It carries a 5-year warranty and is sold by BLUETTI with Amazon shipping.
cons: AC outlet count not stated on the listing

editorial.tagline: The fastest-charging, most powerful 1 kWh station here.
editorial.summary: 2,000 W output from 1,024 Wh, a full recharge in 49 minutes, 600 W solar, a 10 ms UPS and 4,000 cycles to 80% — at the same $500 as rivals with less.
body: Anker's second-generation C1000 raises output to 2,000 W (3,000 W peak), more than any other 1 kWh model here, so it can run a microwave, a coffee maker or a window AC on its own.

HyperFlash charging pulls 1,600 W from the wall and fills the battery in 49 minutes, and 600 W of solar gets it full in about 1.8 hours. A time-of-use mode charges off-peak and powers your devices when electricity costs more.
Owners report running an AirSense 11 CPAP for three nights on a charge and getting through an ice storm with it. At 24.9 lb it's also among the lightest 1 kWh units.
cons: Fast charging must be enabled in the app
editorial.ideal_for: Home backup, CPAP and anyone who wants the most power per dollar at 1 kWh.
editorial.not_for: Buyers who need more than 1 kWh or solar input above 600 W.
editorial.verdict: The best 1 kWh power station you can buy right now.

editorial.tagline: The 1 kWh station that grows to 5 kWh.
editorial.summary: EcoFlow's full DELTA 3: 1,024 Wh, six AC outlets, 13 outputs in total and an expansion port that scales it to 5 kWh. It costs $100 more than the DELTA 3 Classic for that flexibility.
body: The DELTA 3 adds what the Classic leaves out: an extra-battery port (up to 5 kWh with EcoFlow's DELTA 3, DELTA Pro 3 or DELTA 2 Max packs), six AC outlets and an 800 W alternator charging input for vans and RVs.
Output is the same 1,800 W (3,600 W surge), and with wall and solar together it fills in 56 minutes. The battery is rated for 4,000 cycles to 80%, and Amazon sells it directly.
Owners run diesel heaters overnight, fridges on two-night camping trips and coffee makers during outages; several have sent units to family in Cuba for blackouts.
editorial.ideal_for: Buyers who want to start at 1 kWh and add capacity later, and RV owners with alternator charging.
editorial.not_for: Anyone sure they'll never expand — get the Classic.
editorial.verdict: Buy it for the expansion port; otherwise the Classic is the better deal.

products.name: Anker SOLIX S2000

specs_extra.Idle draw: 6 W (Anker) — about 35 h of fridge backup claimed
specs_extra.Outlets: Front and rear AC outlets; no 12 V DC port

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W / 3,000 W peak, 400 W solar, <10 ms UPS, 10,000 cycles, 6 W idle, 35.7 lb, 5-year warranty). Wall charging time isn't stated.

editorial.tagline: 2 kWh for $700 — half the price per Wh of most rivals.
editorial.summary: 2,010 Wh in the smallest, lightest 2 kWh body we've seen (35.7 lb), with a 6 W idle draw, a 10 ms UPS and a 10,000-cycle battery. Output is a modest 1,500 W and solar input stops at 400 W.
body: The S2000 is built for one job — long, efficient backup — and prices it aggressively at about $0.35 per Wh. Anker rates its idle draw at 6 W, which is why it claims up to 35 hours of fridge backup, and its 314 Ah cells for 10,000 cycles.

The trade-offs are 1,500 W of output (enough for a fridge, router, lights and a microwave, not a space heater and microwave together), 400 W of solar, and no 12 V car-style socket. Outlets sit front and back so always-on devices can stay plugged in behind it.
Owners have ridden out 25- and 30-hour outages with it and call it the most efficient 2 kWh unit they've tried; one reports a buggy app. It was the best-selling large station in our check.
editorial.ideal_for: Keeping a fridge, freezer, router and lights running through long outages.
editorial.not_for: Running high-wattage appliances at the same time or big solar setups.
editorial.verdict: The best value in the whole catalog for outage backup.
editorial.review_summary: 4.7★ from 315 ratings (94% 4–5 stars). Owners praise efficiency, size and performance through 25- and 30-hour outages; one says the app is buggy. It sells over 4,000 units a month.

reviews.author: EmbeddedFlyer
reviews.excerpt: More efficient, lighter and smaller than any other 2 kWh unit; a great UPS.

reviews.author: Radovan Bronisevsky

reviews.author: Jason Gallagher

reviews.author: Carl A. Willis

products.name: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max

specs_extra.X-Boost: Runs resistive appliances up to 3,400 W
specs_extra.Solar: Max solar input isn't on the US listing (EcoFlow's EU spec sheet lists 500 W)

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (2,048 Wh, 2,400 W, 3,400 W X-Boost, 0–80% in 1.13 h, <10 ms UPS, 44.8 lb, 5-year warranty) + Backup Power Hub (4,800 W surge, 3,000 cycles to 80%).

editorial.tagline: 2 kWh with enough output for heavy kitchen appliances.
editorial.summary: 2,048 Wh and 2,400 W (4,800 W surge, 3,400 W X-Boost) with a 10 ms UPS and 80% in 68 minutes. More powerful than the Anker S2000, but $180 more and 9 lb heavier.
body: The DELTA 3 Max is EcoFlow's mid-size home backup: 2,048 Wh and 2,400 W, with X-Boost running resistive loads like kettles and heaters up to 3,400 W. That's enough for a fridge, microwave and lights at the same time.

It charges to 80% in about 68 minutes and switches to battery in under 10 ms. EcoFlow doesn't list the solar input on the US listing (its EU spec sheet gives 500 W), and the standard Max isn't expandable — that's the Max Plus.
Owners praise fast charging and long runtime; several bought it for family in Cuba to cope with frequent blackouts.
cons: Solar input not on the US listing
editorial.ideal_for: Outage backup that includes kitchen appliances.
editorial.not_for: Solar-first setups or buyers who want to expand later.
editorial.verdict: A strong 2 kWh unit — pick it over the S2000 only if you need the extra output.
editorial.review_summary: 4.7★ from 609 ratings (94% 4–5 stars). Owners praise fast charging, long battery life and quiet operation, and several use it for family backup in Cuba.

reviews.author: Ariel Diaz
reviews.excerpt: Charges very fast and the battery lasts a long time.

reviews.author: Alexis Coutin
reviews.excerpt: Bought for family in Cuba with frequent outages; they're very happy.

reviews.author: Kenyatta Arnold
reviews.excerpt: Great capacity; charges in a little over an hour.

products.name: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2

specs.charge_note: 0–80% in 66 min; full in 102 min in emergency mode

specs_extra.Firmware: Owners report solar charging needs firmware v1.1

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (2,042 Wh, 2,200 W, 80% in 66 min, 20 ms UPS, 39.5 lb, 5-year warranty) + jackery.com (4,400 W surge, 400 W solar, 4,000 cycles to 70%).

editorial.tagline: Jackery's light 2 kWh unit, with a few rough edges.
editorial.summary: 2,042 Wh and 2,200 W in a 39.5 lb body, three AC outlets and a UL-tested 20 ms UPS. It costs $200 more than the Anker S2000 and has the lowest rating among the 2 kWh units.
body: The Explorer 2000 v2 is a compact 2 kWh station at 39.5 lb, with 2,200 W output (4,400 W surge) and a quiet sub-30 dB charging mode. It reaches 80% in 66 minutes from the wall.
Its weak points are the three AC outlets, 400 W of solar and a 20 ms UPS switch. Owners also report that solar charging needed a firmware update (v1.1) to work properly.

Many owners love it — one lives off-grid in Belize on it — but 9% of ratings are one star, and one engineer measured much less usable capacity than rated because of idle draw. Jackery support gets good marks for replacing a dead unit.
editorial.ideal_for: Jackery fans who want 2 kWh in a portable package.
editorial.not_for: Value shoppers — the Anker S2000 costs $200 less.
editorial.verdict: A capable 2 kWh unit, but hard to recommend over the S2000 at this price.
editorial.review_summary: 4.4★ from 874 ratings (87% 4–5 stars). Owners praise portability, quiet operation and Jackery's support. Complaints include a unit that arrived dead, a firmware update needed for solar, and one owner's measurement of low usable capacity due to idle draw.

specs_extra.Surge: BLUETTI lists 4,800 W; The Solar Lab lists 3,900 W

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (3,014 Wh, 2,400 W / 4,800 W surge, TT-30, 12 V/30 A, 10 ms UPS) + bluettipower.com (6,000+ cycles) + The Solar Lab review (1,200 W solar, 1,800 W AC, 58 lb, charge time, efficiency).

editorial.tagline: 3 kWh with an RV plug, for $1,100.
editorial.summary: 3,014 Wh, 2,400 W, a TT-30 RV outlet and a 12 V/30 A DC port in what BLUETTI calls the smallest 3 kWh station. At $0.36 per Wh it's the cheapest big battery here.
body: The Elite 300 is designed for RVs and home backup. Besides four AC outlets it has a TT-30 plug that feeds an RV's shore-power inlet and a high-current 12 V/30 A DC output for 12 V fridges, water pumps and diesel heaters.
It takes 1,200 W of solar (about three hours to full) or 1,800 W from the wall. The Solar Lab measured about 86% efficiency and ~15 W idle draw, and it switches to battery in 10 ms.
At 58 lb it's heavy but small for 3 kWh. Early owners praise the app and 24/7 support; one early reviewer was disappointed by solar limits at launch before revising to five stars.
cons: Warranty length not on the listing
editorial.ideal_for: RVs, trailers and multi-day home backup.
editorial.not_for: Anyone who needs to carry it often.
editorial.verdict: The best big power station for RVs, and the lowest cost per Wh here.
editorial.review_summary: 4.7★ from 241 ratings (95% 4–5 stars). Owners praise the compact size for 3 kWh, the app, quiet operation and BLUETTI's support. One found solar input limited at launch; another notes it has no server-shutdown communication.

products.name: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus

specs_extra.X-Boost: Runs resistive appliances up to 3,800 W
specs_extra.Expansion: Up to 10 kWh with EcoFlow extra batteries

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (2,048 Wh, 3,000 W, 3,800 W X-Boost, <10 ms UPS, expandable to 10 kWh, 49 lb, 5-year warranty) + ecoflow.com spec sheet (6,000 W surge, 1,000 W solar, 1,800 W AC input, 4 × 20 A outlets, 140 W USB-C).

editorial.tagline: 2 kWh today, 10 kWh later, with 3,000 W of output.
editorial.summary: The DELTA 3 Max with the upgrades that matter for home backup: 3,000 W output (6,000 W surge), 1,000 W solar and an expansion port to 10 kWh. It's the priciest 2 kWh unit here.
body: The Max Plus is built to grow. It starts at 2,048 Wh, but EcoFlow's extra batteries take it up to 10 kWh, and 3,000 W of output (6,000 W surge) handles well pumps, microwaves and window ACs.
It doubles the plain Max's solar input to 1,000 W and switches to battery in under 10 ms. The listing quotes both 43 and 64 minutes to 80%, so expect about an hour.
Owners use it with an extra battery to back up TVs, routers and fans, for car camping with an EV, and for small RVs. With 97 ratings its track record is still short.
editorial.ideal_for: Home backup you plan to expand, and high-draw appliances.
editorial.not_for: Buyers who just want 2 kWh cheaply.
editorial.verdict: Worth it only if you'll use the expansion port and the extra output.
editorial.review_summary: 4.6★ from 97 ratings (88% 4–5 stars). Owners praise build quality, fast charging and quiet operation for home backup, EV camping and RVs. The review base is still small.

specs.charge_note: Full in 2.5 h from the wall, 2 h with AC + solar

specs_extra.240 V: 120/240 V when two units are paired (7,200 W)
specs_extra.Home integration: Plug-and-play with Jackery's transfer switch (sold separately)

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (3,584 Wh, 3,600 W, 6,000 cycles, expandable to 21 kWh, 77.2 lb, 5-year warranty) + The Solar Lab review (7,200 W surge rating, 1,000 W solar, 1,800 W AC, efficiency and idle draw).

editorial.tagline: Real home backup: 3.6 kWh, 3,600 W and a 30 A RV outlet.
editorial.summary: 3,584 Wh and 3,600 W (7,200 W surge) on wheels, expandable to 21.5 kWh and able to feed a home circuit panel through a transfer switch. Heavy, and its idle draw is high.
body: The HomePower 3600 Plus is Jackery's home-backup machine. 3,600 W from four outlets plus a 30 A RV plug runs sump pumps, well pumps, fridges and window ACs, and two units together give 240 V for dryers and central systems.

It refills in 2.5 hours from the wall or about 4 hours on 1,000 W of solar, and expansion packs take it to 21.5 kWh. The Solar Lab measured 89% efficiency but a 34 W idle draw, so switch it off when not in use.
At 77 lb it rolls on wheels rather than being carried. Owners in hurricane country have bought two, and one runs a boat's accessories including the water heater and AC.
pros: 30 A RV outlet, 240 V when paired
editorial.ideal_for: Hurricane and storm prep, whole-circuit home backup and big RVs.
editorial.not_for: Camping or anything you'll lift into a car.
editorial.verdict: The best portable-ish home backup here — plan for its weight and idle draw.
editorial.review_summary: 4.6★ from 194 ratings (92% 4–5 stars). Owners praise capacity, expansion and holding charge in storage, and several own two or three Jackery units for hurricane season. It's heavy.

products.spec_sources: Amazon listing (3,600 Wh LFP, 3,600 W / 7,200 W surge, 1,600 W solar, 1,800 W / 3,000 W AC input, expandable to 25 kWh, 99 lb, 5-year warranty). Cycle rating and UPS time aren't on this listing.

editorial.tagline: The original big EcoFlow: 3.6 kWh that scales to 25 kWh.
editorial.summary: 3,600 Wh and 3,600 W with 1,600 W of solar input, EV-station charging and expansion to 25 kWh. It's older, heavier (99 lb) and pricier than the newest 3 kWh units.
body: The DELTA Pro has been EcoFlow's flagship home battery for years. It delivers 3,600 W from five AC outlets (4,500 W with X-Boost, 7,200 W surge) and a 30 A Anderson port for RV and marine gear.
Its charging options are the widest here: 1,600 W of solar, 3,000 W from a 240 V dryer outlet, even an EV charging station. Extra batteries and a Smart Generator scale it to 25 kWh.

The downsides are age and bulk: 99 lb on wheels, and $1,899 for less capacity per dollar than the BLUETTI Elite 300 or Jackery 3600 Plus. Owners run heat presses at vendor markets and replace noisy gas generators with it.
cons: Solar limited to 15 A per owner feedback
editorial.ideal_for: Large solar setups and homes planning a scalable battery system.
editorial.not_for: Anyone who wants the lowest cost per Wh or needs to move it often.
editorial.verdict: Still capable, but the newer 3 kWh units are better value unless you need its solar and expansion.
